voice_thinking_tone_enabled.hint: A soft tone while Goose works, so the silence does not seem broken.

voice_max_turns.hint: How much work Goose may do before it answers out loud. Zero means no limit.

voice_kws_post_trigger_silence_ms.label: Stop after a pause of
voice_kws_post_trigger_silence_ms.hint: How long a pause means you have finished speaking.

voice_kws_cooldown_ms.label: Wait before listening again
voice_kws_cooldown_ms.hint: How long to wait after answering before listening for its name again.

voice_recording_duration_secs.label: Recording length
voice_recording_duration_secs.hint: How long it records after you speak to it.

voice_whisper_url.label: Transcription service
voice_whisper_url.hint: Address of the service that turns speech into text.

show_thinking.label: Show thinking as it happens
show_thinking.hint: Watch Goose think while it works.

persist_thinking.label: Keep thinking after the reply
persist_thinking.hint: Keep its reasoning so you can open it again later.

goal_check_enabled.label: Check the question was answered
goal_check_enabled.hint: Goose asks itself whether it really answered you, and keeps going if not.

review_max_rounds.label: Revision rounds
review_max_rounds.hint: How many times an answer may be sent back for another try.

review_pass_threshold.label: Pass mark
review_pass_threshold.hint: How good an answer must be, out of 5, to pass the check.

memory_extraction_enabled.label: Learn from conversations
memory_extraction_enabled.hint: Goose reads your conversations back in quiet moments and remembers what lasts. It takes a while to show up.

memory_extraction_max_facts.label: Most things kept at once
memory_extraction_max_facts.hint: How many things it may remember from one stretch of conversation. Fewer is better.

agent_memory_inject.label: Use memories in replies
agent_memory_inject.hint: Let Goose recall what it knows about you when it answers.

agent_memory_limit.label: Memories per reply
agent_memory_limit.hint: How many remembered things it may bring to one answer.

memory_cleanup_enabled.label: Let memories fade
memory_cleanup_enabled.hint: Old memories fade and are tidied away on their own.

memory_consolidation_enabled.label: Merge repeated memories
memory_consolidation_enabled.hint: Merge memories that repeat or contradict each other.

memory_extraction_interval_secs.label: Wait between readings
memory_extraction_interval_secs.hint: The shortest gap between two readings. It only makes them rarer.

memory_decay_base_half_life_days.label: Half-life
memory_decay_base_half_life_days.hint: How long an ordinary memory takes to fade by half. Important ones last longer.

memory_decay_beta.label: Fade curve
memory_decay_beta.hint: How sharply memories fade. Lower is gentler.

memory_archive_threshold.label: Hide below
memory_archive_threshold.hint: How faded a memory must be before it is hidden but kept.

memory_prune_threshold.label: Delete below
memory_prune_threshold.hint: How faded a memory must be before it is deleted.

embedding_provider.label: Search memories by meaning
embedding_provider.hint: Find a memory by what it means, not only the words in it, so a question in English can find a fact said in Swahili. Off, your Pond searches by keyword.

ext_memory_enabled.label: Memories
ext_memory_enabled.hint: Remember, recall and forget things when you ask.

ext_schedule_enabled.label: Schedules
ext_schedule_enabled.hint: Create, pause and run things on a schedule.

ext_knowledge_enabled.label: Knowledge
ext_knowledge_enabled.hint: Look things up in an encyclopedia.

ext_device_enabled.label: Devices
ext_device_enabled.hint: See and change the devices in your home.

ext_sensor_enabled.label: Sensors
ext_sensor_enabled.hint: Read what the sensors in your home have recorded.

ext_travel_enabled.label: Travel
ext_travel_enabled.hint: Make map directions and ride links you open on your phone.

ext_system_enabled.label: System
ext_system_enabled.hint: Read files and check on the machine your Pond runs on.

ext_orchestrator_enabled.label: Delegation
ext_orchestrator_enabled.hint: Hand part of a job to a helper working on its own.

ext_context_enabled.label: Personal context
ext_context_enabled.hint: Read the notes and documents your home has given it.

searxng_url.label: Search server
searxng_url.hint: Address of your own search server, if you run one.

mesh_enabled.label: Talk to your other Ponds
mesh_enabled.hint: Let this Pond work with your other Ponds.

home_name.label: Home name
home_name.hint: What to call this home. Shown in this app.

weather_enabled.label: Use local weather
weather_enabled.hint: Let your Pond know the weather where you are.

vision_enabled.label: Watch the camera
vision_enabled.hint: Look through the camera and note what happens. Needs a camera your Pond can reach.

picture_support_download_enabled.label: Allow picture support downloads
picture_support_download_enabled.hint: Allow downloading vision encoder files (mmproj) for vision-capable models on budgeted devices.

vision_camera_url.label: Camera address
vision_camera_url.hint: A network address, or a camera plugged into your Pond. Leave it empty and your Pond looks for one itself.

vision_camera_id.label: Camera name
vision_camera_id.hint: Used in the activity feed and in automations.

vision_fps.label: Pictures per second
vision_fps.hint: From 1 to 30. More pictures catch quick movement sooner and use more of your Pond; 2 to 5 is enough to notice people.

vision_motion_threshold.label: Motion sensitivity
vision_motion_threshold.hint: How much of the picture must change to count as movement. A lower number notices smaller movements.

vision_classifier_model.label: Detector
vision_classifier_model.hint: What names what the camera saw. Leave empty for the built-in one.

matter_ble_enabled.label: Pair over Bluetooth
matter_ble_enabled.hint: Needed for a brand-new device, which announces itself over Bluetooth first.

unprompted_speech_enabled.label: Speak without being asked
unprompted_speech_enabled.hint: Let Goose speak first when it has news.

proactive_review_enabled.label: Think over the day
proactive_review_enabled.hint: Let Goose review the day on its own. Needs Delegation in Tools.

session_titling_enabled.label: Name conversations
session_titling_enabled.hint: Goose names your conversations while it is idle. It never changes a name you typed.

suggestions_muted.label: Hidden suggestions
suggestions_muted.hint: Kinds of suggestion Home will not offer. Remove one to see it again.

schedule_max_concurrent.label: Tasks at once
schedule_max_concurrent.hint: How many scheduled jobs may run at the same time.

schedule_max_runs_per_task.label: History per task
schedule_max_runs_per_task.hint: How many past runs to keep for each scheduled job.

mic_enabled.label: Microphone
mic_enabled.hint: Off means your Pond cannot hear anything.

context_ingest_enabled.label: Learn from sensors
context_ingest_enabled.hint: Let what the sensors and cameras notice become part of what Goose knows.

telemetry_enabled.label: Record how it performs
telemetry_enabled.hint: Keep a record of how fast Goose answers, on your Pond.

retention_events_days.label: Events
retention_events_days.hint: Days of events to keep, unless a kind below says otherwise.

retention_sensitive_days.label: Anything sensitive
retention_sensitive_days.hint: The longest anything sensitive is kept, whatever the other rules say.

llm_temperature.label: Creativity
llm_temperature.hint: Lower is steadier, higher is more inventive.

llm_max_tokens.label: Longest reply
llm_max_tokens.hint: How long one answer may get.

context_window_override.label: Memory window
context_window_override.hint: Limit how much Goose holds in mind at once. Zero uses the model’s own limit.

agent_max_turns.label: Steps per request
agent_max_turns.hint: How many steps Goose may take on one request before it must answer.

agent_timeout_secs.label: Give up after silence
agent_timeout_secs.hint: How long to wait in silence before giving up on a reply. Zero waits for ever.

prefix_cache_prompt.label: Start replies sooner
prefix_cache_prompt.hint: Reuse the unchanging part of its instructions between replies.

hybrid_compaction_enabled.label: Trim history as you go
hybrid_compaction_enabled.hint: Shorten long conversations as they grow, so they keep fitting.

summary_idle_secs.label: Summarise after idle
summary_idle_secs.hint: How long you must be idle before it summarises the conversation so far.

compaction_verbatim_days.label: Keep in full for
compaction_verbatim_days.hint: Days of conversation kept word for word before shortening.

context_monitor_enabled.label: Warn before it fills
context_monitor_enabled.hint: Warn you before a conversation gets too long to hold.

show_turn_stats.label: Show speed under replies
show_turn_stats.hint: Show how fast each reply was, under the message.

cameras_enabled.label: Cameras
cameras_enabled.hint: Lets your Pond use its camera at all. Off means no watching, no pictures and no face recognition, whatever is set under Cameras and vision.

vision_event_cooldown_secs.label: Pause between events
vision_event_cooldown_secs.hint: After your Pond records something it waits this long before recording anything else, whatever it is.

vision_classifier_confidence.label: How sure before it counts
vision_classifier_confidence.hint: Something the detector is less sure about than this is treated as plain movement.

vision_face_recognition_enabled.label: Recognise faces
vision_face_recognition_enabled.hint: When someone is seen, your Pond checks whether it knows their face.

vision_face_on_motion.label: Look for faces in plain movement too
vision_face_on_motion.hint: Check for a face even when the detector saw only movement. A face found turns the event into a person.

notices_wait_in_quiet_hours.label: Hold notices in quiet hours
notices_wait_in_quiet_hours.hint: In quiet hours, alerts and reminders set for that time still arrive; everything else waits for one notice when quiet hours end.

speak_unfetched_reminders.label: Say a reminder no phone picked up
speak_unfetched_reminders.hint: When no phone fetches a reminder within five minutes, the Pond says it once in the room, outside quiet hours.

unseen_phone_skip_days.label: Stop notifying a phone not seen for

unseen_phone_remove_days.label: Remove a phone not seen for

lone_voice_sets_reminders.label: A voice the Pond does not know may set reminders
lone_voice_sets_reminders.hint: In a household of one, a voice the Pond cannot identify may set reminders and to-dos as that member.

balanced.label: Balanced
balanced.hint: Warm, and gets to the point

concise.label: Concise
concise.hint: As few words as the answer allows

technical.label: Technical
technical.hint: Precise, and assumes you know the terms

q8.label: Balanced
q8.hint: 92 MB. The default, and fits beside the language model.

q8f16.label: Compact
q8f16.hint: 86 MB. The smallest, for a busy Pond.

fp16.hint: 163 MB. Closer to the reference sound.

fp32.label: Reference
fp32.hint: 326 MB. The best sound, slowest, and heavy on memory.

auto.label: When the model can
auto.hint: Goose thinks first on models that support it

on.label: Always try
on.hint: Even on models that usually skip it

brief.label: Brief
brief.hint: Fastest. On a small Pond every moment of thinking is silence before the answer

thorough.label: Thorough
thorough.hint: Best on a powerful machine, slow on a small Pond

auto.label: Factual questions
auto.hint: Only where a wrong answer would matter

on.label: Every answer
on.hint: Slower: every answer is checked first

single.label: One pass
single.hint: Quickest, and lightest on your Pond

all.label: All of them
all.hint: Every tool, every time. Uses about 40% of the room for instructions

relevant.label: The relevant ones
relevant.hint: A small core plus what this conversation seems to need

minimal.label: Only when asked
minimal.hint: Almost nothing until Goose asks for a group of tools

open.label: Open
open.hint: Goose may reach any site. Every request is recorded

allowlist.label: Approved sites only
allowlist.hint: Only the services your Pond needs, from a list built into it

audit.label: Watch
audit.hint: Records every decision and blocks nothing. The usual setting

enforce.label: Enforce
enforce.hint: Refuses what the rules do not allow. Read the activity log first

off.label: Off
off.hint: No checks and no record. For troubleshooting only

privacy.intro: A summary of what happens to your household’s data. The privacy policy below says it in full, and is what counts.
privacy.phoneBody: This phone keeps your Pond’s keys, the session token, the token that renews it and your Pond’s verified identity, in its own protected storage: the Keychain on iPhone and encrypted storage on Android. They are never included in a backup. It also keeps a random identifier made when you installed the app, so your Pond recognises this phone when you pair again, and ordinary preferences such as your Pond’s address and your settings. None of it goes anywhere except to your Pond.
privacy.voiceBody:
When you talk to Goose, in voice mode or from the orb, the app records only while you are speaking and sends those stretches to your Pond, which turns them into text. The copy on this phone is deleted once it is sent, your Pond does not keep the recording, and what you said is kept as text in the conversation.

Listening for your wake word is off unless you turn it on. While it listens, Android shows a notification you cannot hide, and it listens only while this phone is unlocked. “Hey Goose” is recognised on this phone, and nothing is kept or sent until the orb opens. Any other phrase is checked by your Pond, which answers only whether it heard the phrase and keeps neither the recording nor what was said.
privacy.cameraBody:
The camera reads QR codes, your Pond’s pairing code and a device’s setup code, on this phone; no picture is saved or sent. It also takes a photo when you choose to send one to Goose.

When you attach photos or files, the app sees only the ones you pick, never your whole library. A photo is made smaller and saved afresh before it is sent, which leaves out its location and the other details a camera records. All of it goes to your Pond, and nowhere else.
privacy.locationBody:
The app reads your location for four things: three only while it is open, and one in the background, on your phone alone.

A ride: when you ask for a fare, it reads where you are once, and your Pond sends that pickup point to Uber.

Where home is: while this phone is on your home network, and only if you accept, it can tell your Pond where home is, to about 110 metres, so the weather and nearby results are right. Your Pond refuses this from a phone away from home.

Telling Goose where you are, if you turn it on: each message carries the name of the place this phone is in, such as “Westlands, Nairobi”, and never your coordinates.

Places you save for reminders, if you allow location all the time: your phone watches them in the background to remind you when you arrive or leave. Your Pond hears only which place and which way, never where you are.
privacy.bluetoothBody: Bluetooth is used only while you set up a new Pond: to find it, claim it with the code on its setup card, and tell it which Wi-Fi network to join. Your Wi-Fi password goes to the Pond encrypted, and this phone does not keep it. Android is told that Bluetooth is never used to work out where you are, so setting up a Pond does not ask for your location.
privacy.localBody: Your conversations, memories, schedules, devices and household profiles are kept on your Pond, in your home. There is no account with us, and no server of ours holding a copy. The language models your Pond ships with run on the Pond itself, so what you ask Goose is answered at home. We have no access to any of it.
privacy.storageBody:
Keys you give your Pond for other services are encrypted on disk. Your Pond can also keep all of its data, your conversations, memories, profiles, face templates and those keys, in an encrypted volume that its own security chip opens at start-up, with your admin card as the recovery key. Storage taken out of your Pond then shows nothing. Until that is set up, the data is ordinary files, and your Pond’s health check says which it is. On a Pond whose security fuses have not been set, its storage moved into another identical device may still open, so keep the Pond somewhere safe.

This phone and your Pond talk over an encrypted connection. The first time you pair, this phone records your Pond’s identity, and from then on it refuses anything that cannot prove it is that same Pond, at home or away.
privacy.facesBody: If you enrol a face, your Pond makes a numerical template of it and keeps that, never the photo. It is used only to recognise the members of your household on your own cameras. Removing a household member deletes their face template with them.
privacy.networkTitle: What your Pond reaches on the internet
privacy.networkBody:
Some features need the internet, and these connections are your Pond’s, not this app’s. The weather comes from Open-Meteo, encyclopedia lookups from Wikipedia, and music from Spotify once you connect it. Keys you add turn on more: Wolfram|Alpha for calculations, and Brave for web search, which sends your question to Brave and reads the top result pages from their own sites. If you turn on nearby places, each search also sends your town, never your exact location.

Your Pond keeps a record of every outbound call it makes, and can be set to refuse sensitive destinations or to stay offline entirely.
privacy.notificationsBody: When your Pond has something to tell you, it wakes this phone through Google’s notification service, or Apple’s on iPhone. The message is empty: no text and no detail about what happened. This phone then fetches the notification from your Pond directly, so its content never passes through Google, Apple or us.
privacy.remoteBody: Remote access is off unless you turn it on, and your Pond must approve it from your home network. A coordination service we run introduces this phone and your Pond to each other. It learns this phone’s network keys, its private address and when it connects, never what you do. The connection is encrypted end to end, and a relay, when one is needed, carries it already encrypted and cannot read it.
privacy.neverBody:
No analytics, no crash reporting, no advertising or advertising identifier, and no tracking across other apps or websites. The app never reads your contacts.

Two Google components are in the app because it cannot work without them: ML Kit, which reads QR codes on this phone, and Firebase Cloud Messaging, which delivers the empty notifications. Google says they may send it technical information about how they are running, not what you do in the app.

privacy.rightRemoveMember: Remove a household member under Users, and their face template goes with them.
privacy.rightYourData: Everything else is on your Pond, which you own: you delete it there, and we hold no copy to ask for.

## The short version

Goose On The Go is a remote control for a server you own. Almost everything the app does
happens between your phone and that server, and nothing about it passes through us.

We are not a cloud service holding your data. There is no account with us, no analytics,
no advertising, and no third party watching what you do in the app. If you never turn on
remote access, your phone and your Pond never talk to us at all.

One thing you can ask for does reach a company outside your home: a ride. When you ask
Goose for a ride fare, your phone reads where you are once and your Pond passes that pickup
point to Uber, so Uber can price the ride you asked for. That is described below too.

Your Pond itself reaches some services on the internet to do what you ask of it, such as the
weather for where you live or a web search. Those are your Pond's, not this app's, and your
Pond's own settings show and control them.

The rest of this document says exactly what happens when you do turn it on, because a
promise like the one above is only worth anything if the exceptions are stated plainly.

## What stays on your phone

Your phone keeps the credentials for your Pond in the device's own protected storage — the
Keychain on iOS, EncryptedSharedPreferences on Android. That means your session token, the
token used to renew it, your Pond's verified identity, and a random identifier generated on
your phone when you install the app.

That identifier is how your Pond recognises this phone when you pair with it again, instead
of gradually filling up with duplicate entries. It is generated on your device, it is not
derived from anything about your hardware, and it goes nowhere except to your own Pond.

If you choose to open My Pond with your phone's security, your phone also keeps its own key to
My Pond in that protected storage. Only your phone's own check can read it: Face ID or a
fingerprint on an iPhone, a fingerprint or the phone's PIN, pattern or password on Android. It is
never included in a backup or moved to another phone, and adding a new face or fingerprint makes
it unreadable. Forgetting My Pond on this phone, or unpairing it, removes it.

Your phone also keeps ordinary preferences: your Pond's address on your network, which
screen you were last on, your settings. None of this leaves your phone.

## What your Pond receives

Everything the app does functionally — conversations, devices, schedules, everything —
happens between your phone and your Pond, over an encrypted connection that your phone
verifies is really your Pond and not something pretending to be it.

That includes what you choose to give Goose: what you type, what you say when you talk to
it, the photos and files you attach, and, when you ask for a ride fare, where you are. Each
of these is described in its own section below.

Your Pond is your hardware, in your home. Data that reaches it has not left your household,
and we have no access to it.

## Remote access, if you choose it

You can use the app without remote access, and the app will ask rather than assume. If you
decline, nothing in this section happens.

Remote access lets you reach your Pond when you are not at home. To do that, your phone and
your Pond have to be introduced to each other across the internet, and that introduction is
made by a coordination service we operate.

**What that service learns:**

- The cryptographic keys that identify your phone as a device on your own private network.
  These identify a device, not a person.
- The private network address assigned to your phone.
- When your phone connects and disconnects.

**What it does not learn:** anything you do. The connection between your phone and your
Pond is encrypted end to end. The coordination service introduces the two and then is not
part of the conversation. If your phone and your Pond cannot reach each other directly, the
traffic is passed through a relay, which carries it already encrypted and cannot read it.

Turning on remote access also requires approval on the Pond itself, from your home network.
We cannot enable it for you, and neither can anyone who has only your phone.

**Retention:** [NEEDS ANSWER — how long connection records and device keys are kept, and
what happens to them when a phone is unpaired]

## Notifications

When your Pond has something to tell you, it sends your phone a push notification through
Google's or Apple's notification service, because that is the only way to wake an app that
is not running.

Those messages are **empty**. They contain no text and no detail about what happened. Your
phone wakes up, connects to your Pond directly, and fetches the actual content from it.

This is deliberate, and it is the reason the app is built this way: it means the content of
your notifications never passes through Google or Apple. What they see is that your device
was pinged. What was in it, they do not have.

To make this work, your phone gives its notification token to your Pond, and your Pond
talks to Google or Apple directly. We are not in that path either.

## Your voice

**Voice mode.** When you open voice mode to talk to Goose, the app listens through the
microphone for you to speak, and records what you say. Only the stretches where you are
speaking are sent, to your Pond, which turns them into text; the copy on your phone is deleted
as soon as it has been sent. Apart from listening for your wake word, if you turn it on (below),
the microphone is used only while voice mode is open.

**Goose as your phone's assistant (Android).** If you choose Goose as your phone's digital
assistant, holding the side key opens Goose's voice orb over whatever app is open. It listens
in the same way as voice mode, and only while the orb is showing. Over the lock screen, Goose
answers only what needs nothing personal: your memories and notes, messages, calendar, cameras,
sensor history and anything bought or booked wait until you unlock the phone.

**Listening for your wake word (Android, off unless you turn it on).** If you turn on
listening for your wake word, the app listens through the microphone so that saying the phrase
opens the voice orb. While it listens, Android shows a notification that cannot be hidden, and
you can stop it from there. It listens whenever the Goose app is not already open, the lock
screen included.

- If your household's phrase is "Hey Goose", the phone recognises it itself. What it hears
  is checked a fraction of a second at a time and then discarded; nothing is written or sent
  anywhere unless the phone is unsure whether it heard the phrase, when that moment of speech
  goes to your Pond to be checked and nowhere else.
- For any other phrase, only your Pond can recognise it, using the pronunciations it has
  learned from your household. So the phone picks out stretches of speech, at most eight
  seconds each, and sends each one to your Pond, which answers only whether it heard the phrase.
  Your Pond does not keep the recording or what was said, and does not log it. Each stretch is
  held briefly on your phone until your Pond has answered, and is then deleted. This sends
  speech near your phone to your Pond, and nowhere else, which the setting says before you turn
  it on.

If you teach Goose your voice on a phone, that phone keeps, in the app's private storage, a
numerical summary of your voice and a score for each sentence you recorded, never the recording
itself, so that only voices taught on it can wake it. To make that summary it uses your Pond's
voice model, which it fetches from your Pond. Forgetting your voice, in Voice Match or by teaching
it again, deletes it from the phone as well as from your Pond, and uninstalling the app deletes it.
The wake test records you on the phone, scores the recording there, and deletes it; moments it is
unsure of go to your Pond to be checked, as when it listens.

The app does not use the microphone in the background for anything else.

## Camera, photos and files

The app uses your camera for two things.

- **Reading QR codes:** the pairing code your Pond displays, and the setup code on a
  smart-home device you are adding. The code is read on your phone. No photograph is saved,
  and no image is sent anywhere.
- **Taking a photo to send to Goose,** when you choose to.

You can also pick photos from your library, or files, to send to Goose. The app sees only
the photos and files you pick, never your whole library. Before a photo is sent it is made
smaller and saved afresh as a new picture, which leaves out its location and the other
details a camera records about it. A text file is read on your phone and sent as part of
your message. All of it goes to your Pond, and nowhere else.

## Your location

The app reads your location for four things. Three happen only while it is open. The fourth,
watching the places you save for reminders, happens in the background once you allow it, and only
on your phone. It never tracks where you go.

**A ride.** When you ask Goose for a ride fare, the app reads where you are once, precisely
enough for a driver to find you. That reading goes to your Pond, which sends it to Uber as the
pickup point, so Uber can price the ride and, if you confirm it, send a driver. Uber's own
privacy policy covers what Uber does with it. The reading goes from your Pond to Uber
directly; it does not pass through us, and your phone does not keep it after the ride.

**Where home is.** Your Pond has no GPS, so on its own it only knows the city its time zone
names. When your phone reaches your Pond on your home network, and you have already allowed
the app to use your location, the app offers to tell your Pond where home is if your Pond's
location is still only a guess, and does so only if you accept. You can also ask for it with Find
my location in the app. Your phone names the place using its own map service (Google's on
Android, Apple's on iPhone), which is the same service that gives your phone its location. Your Pond keeps the place to about
110 metres, which is enough for the weather and nearby results, and not your exact house. Your
Pond refuses this from a phone that is not on your home network, so a phone away from home can
never move your household.

**Telling Goose where you are (off unless you turn it on).** If you turn on Tell Goose where
this phone is, each message you send carries the name of the place your phone is in, such as
"Westlands, Nairobi", so Goose can say where you are and not only where home is. Only the name
is sent, never your coordinates, and only to your Pond, which uses it for that one message. The
name is looked up at most every five minutes, while you are sending a message.

**Places you save for reminders.** When you save a place for a reminder, such as home or the
office, its position goes to your Pond, which keeps it with your reminders. If you then allow the
app to use your location all the time, your phone watches those places in the background, using
its own geofencing, so it can remind you when you arrive or leave. Your Pond hears only which
saved place it was and whether you arrived or left; where you are never leaves your phone. You can
stop this at any time by turning off location for the app in your phone's settings.

## Bluetooth

The app uses Bluetooth to find a new Pond near you, claim it with the code on its setup card,
and tell it which Wi-Fi network to join. It talks only to the Pond you pick, and only while you
are setting one up. On Android the app tells the system that Bluetooth is never used to work out
where you are, so it does not ask for your location to do this.

The list of Wi-Fi networks comes from your Pond, not from your phone. Your Wi-Fi password goes
from your phone to your Pond encrypted, under a key only the two of them share for that
connection, and your phone does not keep it. Your Pond keeps it the way your computer would, so it
can rejoin the network.

When this phone joins a Pond, it uses its own name (such as "Wanjiru's iPhone"), which you can
change first, so you can tell your devices apart in your Pond's list. That name goes to your Pond
and nowhere else.

## Security

- **Your connection to your Pond** is encrypted. The first time you pair, your phone records
  your Pond's identity, and from then on it refuses to talk to anything that cannot prove it is
  that same Pond, at home or away.
- **Your Pond's keys on this phone** (the session token, the token that renews it, your Pond's
  identity, and this phone's key to My Pond if you use one) are kept in the phone's own
  protected storage: the Keychain on iOS and encrypted storage on Android. They are not included
  in backups.
- **Remote access** is encrypted end to end between your phone and your Pond, and must be
  approved on your Pond, from your home network, before it works.
- **On your Pond**, the keys you give it for other services are stored encrypted. Your Pond can
  also keep all of its data (conversations, memories, profiles, face templates and those keys) in
  an encrypted volume, opened at start-up by your Pond's own security chip, with your admin card as
  the recovery key; then storage taken out of your Pond and read elsewhere shows nothing. Until the
  volume is set up, that data is ordinary files on your Pond, and your Pond's health check says
  which it is. On a Pond whose security fuses have not been set, its storage moved into another
  identical device may still open, so keep your Pond somewhere safe, as you would a computer.

No system is perfectly secure. If you believe your Pond or this phone has been compromised,
unpair this phone, remove it on your Pond's dashboard, and pair again.

## Where your data is processed

Your conversations, your household's data and the content of your notifications are processed
on your Pond, in your home. They do not travel to us, or to any server of ours, in any country.

The coordination service for remote access, if you turn it on, runs on servers we operate in
[NEEDS ANSWER: the countries where the coordination service and its relays run]. The records it
keeps are described under Remote access above.

## What we do not do

- We do not use any analytics service, and the app's own code collects no usage data.
- We do not use crash-reporting or attribution services.
- We do not serve advertising, and we do not use an advertising identifier.
- We do not read your contacts.
- We do not read your location except for the four uses described above, and in the background
  only to watch the places you saved for reminders, on your phone.
- We do not use the microphone except while you talk to Goose, or while listening for your wake
  word if you turn that on, which Android always shows in a notification.
- We do not look through your photo library. The app sees only the photos you pick.
- We do not track you across other apps or websites, and we never will.

These are not intentions: none of them is in the app's own code. Two components from Google
are in the app because it cannot work without them, and they report on their own operation:
**ML Kit**, which reads QR codes on your phone, and **Firebase Cloud Messaging**, which delivers
the app's empty wake-up notifications. Google documents that these can send Google technical
information about how they are working, such as their performance and errors, and not what you
do in the app. [NEEDS ANSWER: confirm on a release build what ML Kit and Firebase send, and
whether the app can turn it off, before publishing.]

## Children

The app is not directed at children. [NEEDS ANSWER — confirm the age rating being submitted
to each store, so this section matches it]

## Your choices and your rights

- **Decline remote access.** The app works without it, and you can turn it down when asked.
- **Turn it off later.** Unpairing releases this phone's access to your Pond, including
  its remote access. You pair again at home to come back. Turning remote access off also
  erases the map of your home network that your phone kept to reconnect quickly.
- **Remove a Pond you cannot reach.** If your Pond does not answer when you unpair, you
  can remove it from this phone instead. The phone forgets the Pond and everything it kept
  from your household; the Pond still lists the phone until you remove it on the Pond's
  dashboard.
- **Your data is on your own hardware.** Deleting it is something you do on your Pond, not
  something you ask us for. We do not hold a copy.

## 2. What the app is

The app is a way to talk to and control a Goose In A Pond device ("your Pond"): a computer you

schedules and information. The app works with your Pond; it does not replace it, and most of what

Remote access lets the app reach your Pond when you are away from home. It is optional, and you

## 6. Goose's answers and actions

Goose is an AI assistant. Its answers are generated by a language model running on your Pond, and
they can be incomplete, out of date, or wrong, even when they sound confident.

- Do not rely on Goose for medical, legal, financial, safety or other professional advice, or for
  decisions where a mistake could cause harm. Check anything important with a reliable source or a
  qualified person.
- When you ask Goose to act, for example to change a device, set a schedule, or book a ride,
  check that it did what you meant. Goose may ask you to confirm before an action; confirming is
  your decision.
- Do not use Goose, or a device it controls, as the only safeguard for anything where failure
  could hurt someone, such as a lock, an alarm, heating, or a medical device.

reserved.title: Reserved address (paid plans)
reserved.help: On ngrok's free plan the address changes every time the tunnel starts, such as when your Pond restarts. A reserved TCP address, on the Hobbyist and Pay-as-you-go plans, never changes, so you can switch to ngrok from anywhere. In the ngrok dashboard open Gateway, then TCP Addresses, create one and paste it here.
